# Style References in AI Image Tools: A Plain-English Explainer

> **In short:** Style references are a feature in modern AI image tools — including Recraft and Picsart — where you upload a picture you like and the AI tries to make new images that feel like it. They help when you want a whole set of images to look like one family.

Have you ever made one AI picture you loved, then tried to make a second one "in the same style" and ended up with something that looked like a distant cousin? Same general idea, totally different vibe.

That's exactly the problem style-reference features are built to fix.

## What a style reference actually does

A style reference is a picture you hand the AI as a visual example. Instead of describing the look only with words in your prompt (the instruction you type to the AI), you're showing it. The AI then tries to carry over the *feel* of your reference — colors, textures, lighting mood, line weight, how painterly or how clean it feels — into whatever new picture you ask it to make.

Think of it like showing a friend a photo and saying, "Make me a poster that feels like this." They don't copy the photo; they borrow the vibe.

## How the controls usually work

Image generators that offer this — including Recraft (a standalone AI image platform) and the AI image tools inside Picsart — generally give you some way to dial in how closely the AI should follow your example. The exact sliders, buttons, and labels differ from tool to tool, so it's worth opening whichever app you use and seeing what's currently there. The underlying idea, though, is usually one of these:

- **Stick closer to the reference.** Colors, textures, and overall mood stay close. Great when consistency matters more than creativity.
- **Use it as loose inspiration.** The AI keeps the general vibe but is freer to vary details. Useful when you want a coherent *series* without every picture looking identical.

If you've ever picked a paint color at a hardware store and seen the "match exactly" button versus the "in the family" button — it's the same idea in image form.

Because the controls and labels shift as tools update, I'd rather point you to the current help page in whichever app you use than name specific menu items that may already be different.

## Picking a good reference

The reference image does most of the heavy lifting, so a little thought goes a long way:

- **Pick something close to your goal.** If you want flat, graphic illustrations, don't feed it a moody oil painting.
- **Clean references work better.** A busy collage of unrelated styles forces the AI to average everything into mush.
- **One strong image often beats five mixed ones.** More references can help, but only if they share a clear visual thread.

## What this means for you

- **If you're making social posts or a lookbook:** A style reference lets you knock out a whole week's content in one sitting and have it look like it came from one designer — instead of seven different ones having a fight.
- **If you run a small business:** You can build a brand look — say, soft pastels for a bakery, or clean line-art for a tech blog — and reuse it across product shots, flyers, and Instagram stories without re-explaining the vibe each time.
- **If you're just experimenting for fun:** Treat the reference like a mood board. Save the ones you like and notice what they have in common — that hidden pattern is your personal style, and the AI can hold onto it for you.

## Wrap-up

Style-reference tools are one of the quietest upgrades in AI image generation: they don't make a single image better, they make a *set* of images feel like one voice — which is exactly why they matter if you've ever been frustrated by AI art that looks like a different artist made every piece. Your move today: pick one reference image you love, try it in whichever image generator you already use, and see whether the next few outputs feel like a family.
